newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Court decision on hotel seen hurting Philippines.
newsitem.headline: Court decision on hotel seen hurting Philippines.

text.p: The Philippines has taken a huge step backwards in its attempts to attract overseas investment with Monday's Supreme Court decision to overturn the sale of the historic Manila Hotel to a Malaysian firm, analysts said.

A 15-judge panel of the court, saying the government should abide by a "Filipino First" policy, awarded the sale of the state-owned hotel to the local Manila Prince Hotel Corp, overturning the winning bid of Renong Berhad in 1995.

Prince, which had challenged the award saying the Manila Hotel was a national treasure, later matched Renong's bid of 673.20 million pesos ($25.6 million), or 44 pesos per share, for a 51 percent stake in the hotel.

It was the latest in a series of high-profile privatisation projects to be reversed by or mired in litigation and some analysts said it reflected a worrying trend of courts becoming involved in economic policy-making.

They said it was a major barrier to investing in the Philippines, which, since economic reforms were launched in 1992, has largely opted for privatisation contracts to upgrade its creaking infrastructure.

"Obviously, if decisions can be reversed after they have been made, investors will be rather concerned," said Guillermo Luz, executive director of the Makati Business Club, the country's most influential grouping of businessmen. "Even local investors will be rather concerned about how long a decision can stick.
"Why waste the time of international bidders if it (the Filipino First policy) is going to be the case," he added. "This type of intervention is worrisome."

On Friday, the Court of Appeals temporarily halted the privatisation of the Manila waterworks system, which had been awarded in January, in response to a petition by a citizens group which said President Fidel Ramos's powers to sell off the utility had lapsed.
The two 25-year contracts to run the waterworks were estimated to involve investment of $7 billion and it was to be one of the biggest water privatisations in the world.
"How far can the courts intervene in economic projects of the executive without usurping executive prerogatives and hampering economic objectives?" said analyst Amando Doronila in a newspaper column.
"The resort to the courts to abrogate public contracts reveals a tenacious mentality in which imagined individual rights violations ride roughshod over public policy," the article added.
The government has said the involvement of the courts is testimony to their independence and the rule of law in the Philippines, which in itself is a powerful attraction to foreign investors.

Asked about a possible loss of investor confidence because of the number of contracts which did not come to fruition despite bids being awarded, Ramos said on Friday: "I don't know if it is growing, but (it) is negated by the fact that investments into the Philippines have grown considerably in 1996 over 1995 and ... we can expect the same kind of momentum to continue in 1997.
"We are going through a process which is unique in our country," he added. "What people are probably missing is the great majority of contracts that are not being questioned but are being upheld."
"The problem is losers (of contracts) in this country have any number of mechanisms to throw a spanner in the works," said a Western diplomat.

A contract to develop reclaimed land in Manila Bay has been held up because the Senate has questioned the compensation paid to the government and Ramos himself stepped in to order fresh bidding in the privatisation of a container port in Subic Bay.

Alex Magno, a professor of political science at the University of the Philippines, said Monday's court decision "sends the wrong signals that bidding rules can be overriden by a judicial system that is still trapped in old nationalist demagoguery".
"We need to act quickly to assure investors that bidding rules are the complete framework on which contracts are awarded."
